h-stakeholder-overview.title: Stakeholder Management key concepts, trends (broader definitions, co-creation), tailoring and agile considerations
h-stakeholder-overview.notes: Every project has stakeholders who impact or are impacted, positively or negatively, with limited to significant influence. Research and high-profile failures show the value of structured identification, prioritisation and engagement of all stakeholders - correct identification and engagement can decide success or failure. Start as soon as possible after the charter is approved, the PM is assigned and the team forms. Stakeholder satisfaction should be identified and managed as a project objective. Key to engagement: continuous communication with all stakeholders, including team members, to understand needs, address issues, manage conflicting interests and foster appropriate engagement. The process is iterative: review and update identification, prioritisation and engagement routinely, and at least when the project moves through phases, when stakeholders leave or join the community, or when there are significant changes in the organisation or wider community. Trends: broader definitions (beyond employees, suppliers, shareholders: regulators, lobby groups, environmentalists, financial organisations, the media, and those who simply believe they are stakeholders); identifying all stakeholders; involving all team members in engagement; reviewing the stakeholder community regularly, often alongside risk reviews; co-creation - consulting the most affected stakeholders and including them in the team as partners; capturing the value of engagement - positive (benefits of active support, especially from powerful stakeholders) and negative (true cost of poor engagement - recalls, reputational loss). Tailoring: stakeholder diversity, complexity of relationships (more networks means more complex flows of information and misinformation), communication technology. Agile: high change requires active engagement; adaptive teams engage stakeholders directly rather than through layers of management; client, user and developer co-create, increasing involvement and satisfaction; regular interaction mitigates risk, builds trust and enables earlier, cheaper adjustment; aggressive transparency - inviting stakeholders to meetings and reviews and posting artefacts publicly to surface misalignment, dependencies or issues quickly. ITTOs for 13.1-13.4 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 13-1.

h-13.1-identify-stakeholders.title: 13.1 Identify Stakeholders: stakeholder analysis and stakes, mapping models (grids, cube, salience, directions of influence), stakeholder register
h-13.1-identify-stakeholders.notes: Identify stakeholders regularly and analyse and document their interests, involvement, interdependencies, influence and potential impact on success; key benefit: the right focus for engaging each stakeholder or group; performed periodically as needed. Often first done before or alongside chartering; repeat at the start of each phase and with significant change, consulting plan components and documents each time. Inputs: charter (key stakeholder list, responsibilities); business documents (first iteration - business case objectives and initial stakeholder list; benefits management plan - beneficiaries); plan (not available initially; later the communications management plan and stakeholder engagement plan); documents (unlikely initially; later change log - new stakeholders or changed relationships, issue log, requirements documentation); agreements (parties are stakeholders and may reference others); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance; standards, regulations, codes of conduct; trends; geographic distribution); OPAs (stakeholder register templates, registers from previous projects, lessons learned about stakeholder preferences). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power structures, culture and environment, industry, team members' expertise); data gathering - questionnaires and surveys (one-on-one reviews, focus groups, mass collection), brainstorming and brain writing (participants consider the question individually before the group session; face-to-face or virtual); data analysis - stakeholder analysis (list with positions, roles, stakes, expectations, attitudes/levels of support, interest in information; stakes include interest (affected by decisions or outcomes), rights - legal (e.g., occupational health and safety) or moral (protecting historical sites, environmental sustainability), ownership (legal title to an asset), knowledge (specialist knowledge or knowledge of power structures), contribution (funds, resources, advocacy, buffering the project from organisational politics)); document analysis; data representation - stakeholder mapping/representation: power/interest, power/influence or impact/influence grids (group by authority, concern about outcomes, ability to influence outcomes or cause changes; suit small projects or simple relationships); stakeholder cube (three-dimensional refinement of the grids, aids communication strategies); salience model (power, urgency - need for immediate attention due to time constraints or high stakes, legitimacy - appropriateness of involvement; an adaptation substitutes proximity for legitimacy; suits large complex communities and helps determine relative importance); directions of influence (upward - senior management, sponsor, steering committee; downward - the team and temporary specialists; outward - suppliers, government departments, public, end users, regulators; sideward - peers such as other PMs or middle managers competing or collaborating over resources); prioritisation (for many stakeholders, frequently changing membership or complex relationships); meetings (facilitation workshops, guided small-group discussions, virtual groups with social media). Outputs: stakeholder register - identification information (name, position, location, contact details, project role), assessment information (major requirements, expectations, potential influence, phase of greatest influence or impact), stakeholder classification (internal/external; impact/influence/power/interest; upward/downward/outward/sideward; or another model); change requests (none in the first iteration; later new stakeholders or information may require changes); plan updates (none at the very beginning; later requirements, communications, risk and stakeholder engagement plans); document updates (assumption log - power, interest and engagement information is largely assumption-based, plus constraints on interacting with stakeholders; issue log; risk register). Data flow: charter from 4.1; agreements from 12.2; change requests to 4.6.

h-13.2-plan-engagement.title: 13.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement: update triggers, prioritisation, engagement assessment matrix (unaware to leading), stakeholder engagement plan
h-13.2-plan-engagement.notes: Develop approaches to involve stakeholders based on needs, expectations, interests and potential impact; key benefit: an actionable plan for effective interaction; performed periodically as needed. First version after initial identification; developed early and updated as the community changes. Update triggers: start of a new phase; changes in organisation structure or industry; stakeholders joining or leaving or their importance changing; outputs of change, risk or issue management requiring a strategy review - possibly changing stakeholders' relative importance. Inputs: charter (purpose, objectives, success criteria); plan (resource management plan - roles; communications management plan - strategies are both inputs to and recipients of stakeholder processes; risk management plan - thresholds and attitudes help choose the strategy mix); documents (assumption log; change log - stakeholders request, decide on or are affected by changes; issue log; project schedule - activities owned or executed by stakeholders; risk register - owners or affected parties; stakeholder register); agreements (coordinate with procurement/contracting to manage contractors and suppliers); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance, personnel policies, stakeholder risk appetites, channels, trends, geography); OPAs (social media, ethics, security policies; issue, risk, change and data management policies; communication requirements; information guidelines; lessons learned on stakeholder preferences; software tools for engagement). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power inside and outside, culture, analytical techniques, communication strategies, knowledge of stakeholders from previous projects); benchmarking (compare stakeholder analysis with world-class organisations or projects); data analysis - assumption and constraint analysis (tailor strategies), root cause analysis (underlying reasons for a stakeholder's level of support, to pick a strategy that improves engagement); decision making - prioritisation/ranking (requirements and stakeholders; those with most interest and highest influence often at the top); data representation - mind mapping (stakeholder information and relationships), stakeholder engagement assessment matrix (compares current with desired engagement; levels: unaware - unaware of the project and impacts; resistant - aware but resistant to change, unsupportive; neutral - aware, neither supportive nor unsupportive; supportive - aware and supportive; leading - aware and actively engaged in ensuring success; C = current, D = desired; the gap directs the communication needed and closing it is essential to monitoring engagement; Figure 13-6 verified example: stakeholder 1 C = unaware, D = supportive; stakeholder 2 C = neutral, D = supportive; stakeholder 3 C and D both supportive - no gap); meetings. Output: stakeholder engagement plan (plan component identifying strategies and actions to promote productive involvement in decision making and execution; formal or informal, detailed or broad; specific strategies for individuals or groups). Data flow: charter from 4.1; agreements from 12.2.

h-13.3-manage-engagement.title: 13.3 Manage Stakeholder Engagement: activities, inputs, communication and interpersonal skills (part 1)
h-13.3-manage-engagement.notes: Communicate and work with stakeholders to meet needs and expectations, address issues and foster appropriate involvement; key benefit: increase support and minimise resistance; performed throughout. Activities: engage stakeholders at appropriate stages to obtain, confirm or maintain commitment; manage expectations through negotiation and communication; address risks or concerns related to stakeholder management and anticipate future issues; clarify and resolve identified issues. Helps stakeholders understand goals, objectives, benefits, risks and how their contribution enhances success. Inputs: plan (communications management plan - methods, formats, technologies; risk management plan - categories, appetites, reporting formats; stakeholder engagement plan - guidance on managing expectations; change management plan - submitting, evaluating, implementing changes); documents (change log - communicated to stakeholders, issue log - concerns and action items, lessons learned, stakeholder register); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance, personnel policies, stakeholder risk thresholds, channels, trends, geography); OPAs (social media, ethics, security; issue, risk, change, data management; communication requirements; information guidelines; historical information). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power, culture, analytical techniques, communication strategies, stakeholder characteristics from previous projects, requirements, vendor and change management); communication skills - apply methods from the communications plan and use feedback to understand stakeholder reactions (formal and informal conversations, issue identification and discussion, meetings, progress reporting, surveys); interpersonal skills - conflict management (resolve conflicts in a timely manner), cultural awareness, negotiation (achieve support or agreement and resolve conflicts), observation/conversation (stay in touch with work and attitudes), political awareness (power relationships within and around the project).
